Check the current order, pump settings and delivered volume
Ask the prescriber to rewrite the infusion prescription
why: The remembered rate may have been superseded; confirm the current prescription.
A new device at an unverified rate can reproduce the error.
Verification establishes the intended rate and possible exposure so treatment can be safely corrected.
A new prescription may not be needed if the current order resolves the discrepancy.
takeaway: Investigate a device setting discrepancy immediately.
learningObjective: Investigate a device setting discrepancy immediately.

title: Alarm fatigue pattern
stem: A monitored client is breathing comfortably with unchanged observations. The oxygen-saturation trace disappears when a visibly loose finger sensor moves, then returns when it is held correctly. What should the nurse do next?
options: Reduce the alarm volume to the night setting
Lower the saturation threshold for this client
Request a different monitor for the bedside
Secure or replace the sensor and verify the signal
why: Volume adjustment does not resolve the lost signal or preserve reliable detection.
Changing a clinical threshold does not correct a contact problem.
The movement-related contact failure should be corrected before attributing it to the whole monitor.
The observed contact problem explains the artifact; correcting it and confirming readings restores monitoring.
takeaway: Resolve nuisance-alarm causes without removing needed safeguards.
learningObjective: Resolve nuisance-alarm causes without removing needed safeguards.

title: Transport oxygen supply
stem: A client needs oxygen during a longer-than-usual transfer. What must be verified?
options: Adequate supply and functioning delivery for the expected trip plus contingency
That the cylinder was replaced at the start of the shift
That oxygen flows when the valve is opened briefly
That the previous client used the cylinder briefly
why: Trip planning must account for consumption and possible delay.
Earlier replacement does not establish enough remaining supply for this trip.
A brief flow check does not establish duration or contingency capacity.
Previous use does not quantify what remains.
takeaway: Check transport support capacity before leaving the care area.
learningObjective: Check transport support capacity before leaving the care area.

title: Tubing misconnections
stem: Several tubes lie together beneath bedding before reconnection after transfer. What is the safest approach?
options: Match tubing by approximate diameter
Trace each line from client to source before connecting
Use the closest available connector
Ask which line was disconnected last
why: Similar diameters do not establish function.
Tracing confirms the intended route and prevents misconnections.
Physical fit alone does not guarantee the correct route.
Sequence memory does not verify line identity.
takeaway: Trace lines fully before connecting them.
learningObjective: Trace lines fully before connecting them.

title: MRI screening gap
stem: A client arrives for MRI and mentions an implanted device not documented on the screening form. What next?
options: Proceed if no device symptoms exist
Ask the client to remove jewellery only
Pause and notify MRI staff for device-specific verification
Use the previous CT screening results
why: Absence of symptoms does not establish MRI compatibility.
Jewellery removal does not address an implanted device.
MRI staff must verify the specific device and conditions.
CT screening does not assess magnetic-field hazards.
takeaway: Resolve implant uncertainty before MRI exposure.
learningObjective: Resolve implant uncertainty before MRI exposure.

title: Equipment recall
stem: A manufacturer notice directs removal of pumps with serial numbers 4100–4199 because the startup test may miss a fault. A nurse is assigned to implement the notice. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Match unit serial numbers against the affected range
Clear an affected pump after a successful startup test
Arrange checked replacement pumps for affected infusions
Return unaffected pumps of the same model for testing
Record the affected device identifiers and actions taken
why: The defined range identifies which devices require the recall response.
The notice specifically states that the startup test may not detect this fault.
Replacement planning avoids creating an interruption while affected devices are removed.
The stated notice does not require withdrawing unaffected devices.
Documented identification and action support traceability and completion of the response.
takeaway: Manage recalls through device identification and safe continuity.
learningObjective: Manage recalls through device identification and safe continuity.

title: Wrong-client screen
stem: A nurse opens a chart to administer treatment but the displayed birth date differs from the wristband. What next?
options: Trust the room assignment
Resolve the identity mismatch before proceeding
Use the first name alone
Ask the client if they recognize the treatment
why: Room assignment is not a reliable identifier.
A mismatch must be clarified before care is linked to a record.
First names may be shared.
Treatment familiarity cannot establish identity.
takeaway: Stop when clinical identifiers conflict.
learningObjective: Stop when clinical identifiers conflict.

title: Specimen label mismatch
stem: A collected specimen label does not match the client's verified identifiers. The collector has left the bedside. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace the label using the chart currently open
Confirm the intended client with the collector by telephone
Contact the laboratory for the approved correction or recollection process
Send the specimen with a note describing the discrepancy
why: An open chart does not establish the identity of the specimen in the tube.
The collector may contribute information, but a recollection or correction decision must preserve the approved identification process.
The laboratory process determines whether identity can be securely corrected or the sample must be recollected.
Processing an unresolved identity discrepancy risks misdirected results and treatment.
takeaway: Resolve specimen identity errors before laboratory processing.
learningObjective: Resolve specimen identity errors before laboratory processing.

title: Surgical-site discrepancy
stem: Before an elective procedure, the consent and site marking name different sides. What is the best action?
options: Use the visible site mark to guide preparation
Use the side recorded on the operating schedule
Confirm the side with the awake client and amend the mark
Pause until the procedural team reconciles the intended site
why: The mark itself may be the incorrect element.
Scheduling information can also contain an error.
Client confirmation is important evidence, but the team must reconcile consent, records and marking before progression.
A coordinated pause resolves conflicting evidence and prevents wrong-site treatment.
takeaway: Resolve procedure and site discrepancies before starting.
learningObjective: Resolve procedure and site discrepancies before starting.

title: Allergy wristband conflict
stem: A client with a confirmed latex allergy is prepared for a scheduled procedure, but latex supplies are on the tray. What should the nurse arrange before proceeding?
options: Replace the latex-containing supplies with suitable alternatives
Cover exposed latex components with a sterile drape
Administer the prescribed antihistamine before using the tray
Increase allergy observations during the procedure
why: Avoiding the known allergen addresses the preventable exposure.
A cover does not reliably eliminate exposure from latex-containing equipment.
Premedication does not make known allergen exposure safe.
Observation may detect a reaction but does not prevent the avoidable exposure.
takeaway: Reconcile allergy information with actual equipment and supplies.
learningObjective: Reconcile allergy information with actual equipment and supplies.

title: Hazardous spill
stem: An unidentified chemical spills beside a treatment area. What is the safest initial approach?
options: Absorb the spill with standard disposable towels
Restrict access and activate the spill response
Dilute the spill with a container of water
Move the nearby treatment supplies to another shelf
why: Absorption methods and protection depend on the chemical hazard.
Access control prevents additional exposure while trained staff identify and manage the spill.
Water can be incompatible with some chemicals.
Protecting supplies does not first protect people from the unidentified spill.
takeaway: Identify and contain chemical hazards through the approved response.
learningObjective: Identify and contain chemical hazards through the approved response.

title: Safety data sheet
stem: A nurse checks the supplied safety summary before using an unfamiliar disinfectant. Which preparations follow these instructions? Select all that apply.
options: Use the specified chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection
Add water to reduce the vapour from this ready-to-use product
Work in the designated ventilated cleaning area
Combine it with the usual bleach solution for stronger cleaning
Locate the eyewash and the product exposure instructions
why: The summary specifies hand and eye protection for splash and contact hazards.
The supplied instructions identify the product as ready to use; an improvised dilution changes its intended preparation.
The designated ventilated area follows the stated inhalation precaution.
The summary explicitly prohibits mixing with bleach.
A known eyewash location and accessible instructions support prompt exposure response.
takeaway: Use safety information before handling unfamiliar hazardous products.
exhibit: Ready to use; do not dilute
Specified chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection
Begin eyewash promptly; obtain medical assistance
learningObjective: Use safety information before handling unfamiliar hazardous products.

title: Chemical eye exposure
stem: A cleaning agent splashes into a worker's eye. A colleague is obtaining the product information and calling for assistance. What should begin immediately?
options: Telephone occupational health for an appointment
Retrieve the product safety data sheet
Begin irrigation at the emergency eyewash
Remove the worker's contaminated outer clothing
why: Calling for assistance is already underway and should not delay eye decontamination.
A colleague is obtaining this information while exposure must be stopped.
Prompt irrigation reduces ongoing eye exposure while product-specific guidance is obtained.
Clothing decontamination may be required, but it does not first remove the chemical from the affected eye.
takeaway: Begin prompt eye irrigation after chemical exposure.
learningObjective: Begin prompt eye irrigation after chemical exposure.

title: Compressed cylinder transport
stem: A transport oxygen cylinder does not fit securely in the stretcher's installed holder. Which arrangement should be used for the transfer?
options: Place it in the stretcher's equipment basket
Have the escort carry it beside the stretcher
Use a similar holder designed for a smaller cylinder
Use an approved carrier that secures this cylinder
why: A general basket may not restrain a cylinder against movement or impact.
Hand carrying does not provide the designed restraint for transport.
A superficially similar holder does not establish a secure compatible fit.
The carrier must be compatible and secure the cylinder during movement.
takeaway: Secure compressed gas cylinders using designed transport equipment.
learningObjective: Secure compressed gas cylinders using designed transport equipment.

title: Hot-water testing
stem: A client with reduced sensation requires bathing. Unit policy requires checking water with a bath thermometer before contact. Which check should guide water safety?
options: Measure the water using the bath thermometer
Ask the client whether a hand in the water feels comfortable
Test the water briefly using the nurse's hand
Confirm that the tap remains at its preset position
why: The required objective check protects a client whose temperature perception is unreliable.
Reduced sensation limits the usefulness of the client's subjective response.
A brief hand test is subjective and does not meet the stated measuring method.
The tap setting does not confirm the temperature actually delivered.
takeaway: Use reliable temperature checks when sensation is impaired.
learningObjective: Use reliable temperature checks when sensation is impaired.

title: Heating-device risk
stem: A client with longstanding neuropathy describes an uncomfortable cold feeling in a numb foot. Skin is intact, colour and pulses are unchanged, and the foot is warm to touch. Which comfort measure is safest while the symptom plan is reviewed?
options: Apply a heating pad on its lowest setting
Use a loose dry sock and reassess comfort
Wrap a hot-water bottle in a towel beside the foot
Prepare a warm foot soak for the client
why: A low setting can still burn insensate skin before discomfort is recognized.
A nonthermal insulating measure avoids exposing numb tissue to an uncontrolled heat source.
Wrapping does not reliably prevent prolonged heat injury in insensate tissue.
Reduced sensation makes excessive water heat harder to detect.
takeaway: Reduced sensation increases risk from therapeutic heat.
learningObjective: Reduced sensation increases risk from therapeutic heat.

title: Hospital-acquired injury review
stem: Adhesive removal leaves a visible skin flap on a frail client's forearm. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the flap, bleeding, pain and surrounding skin
Add adhesive allergy to the client's alert record
Protect the wound according to the assessed wound-care plan
Use the same adhesive to anchor routine dry gauze
Review adhesive choice and removal technique before the next dressing
why: The visible tissue disruption needs a focused assessment to guide care.
A skin tear after removal may reflect mechanical trauma; it does not by itself establish an allergy.
The wound should be protected using care matched to its assessed condition.
Repeating a traumatic adhesive approach may cause further damage; dressing and securement should be reassessed.
Changing a contributing product or technique can reduce recurrence.
takeaway: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.
learningObjective: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.

title: Bed entrapment gap
stem: A replacement mattress creates a large gap beside the bed rail for a frail client. The manufacturer confirms this mattress is incompatible and no approved gap insert exists. Which is the best ongoing solution?
options: Fill the gap with firm pillows beneath the sheet
Request a custom foam insert from maintenance
Replace the setup with compatible approved equipment
Lower the rail and schedule closer observation
why: Pillows can shift and are not a validated entrapment correction.
An improvised insert does not establish a tested safe configuration.
Approved compatible components correct the known equipment mismatch.
Closer observation may support temporary safety arrangements but does not correct the unsuitable equipment for ongoing use.
takeaway: Assess compatibility when bed components change.
learningObjective: Assess compatibility when bed components change.

title: Accessible call system
stem: A client cannot press a standard call button because of severe hand weakness. Speech is faint, but the client reliably moves one knee against a switch during assessment. Which adjustment best supports independent calls for help?
options: Arrange a voice-activated call device
Move the standard button onto the client's lap
Schedule additional staff rounding visits
Provide a suitable knee-activated call switch
why: The client's faint speech may not reliably activate a voice device.
Moving the same button does not overcome inability to press it.
Rounding supplements assistance but does not give the client an independent immediate signal.
The demonstrated movement can activate an adapted switch; successful use should be verified in the usual position.
takeaway: Verify that the client can actually activate the call system.
learningObjective: Verify that the client can actually activate the call system.

title: Post-sedation escort
stem: A client remains drowsy after procedural sedation and plans to leave alone by public transit. The discharge protocol requires adequate recovery and a responsible escort. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Continue monitored recovery and arrange an appropriate escort
Book a taxi to take the client directly home
Ask transit staff to assist the client onto the bus
Provide written directions and a follow-up telephone call
why: Persistent drowsiness requires further recovery assessment, and the stated escort requirement must be met.
A taxi driver does not supply the responsible post-sedation escort or establish adequate recovery.
Transit assistance does not meet recovery and escort requirements.
Written directions and later contact do not address present impairment during travel.
takeaway: Discharge safety includes recovery status and practical support.
learningObjective: Discharge safety includes recovery status and practical support.

title: Sleep position teaching
stem: A parent places a healthy infant on the side for sleep because they fear choking. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Keep side-lying with a rolled towel
Place the infant on the back for each sleep
Use prone positioning after feeds
Alternate positions each night
why: Side positioning is unstable and a roll adds a hazard.
Back positioning is the recommended routine sleep position.
Prone sleep increases risk for a healthy infant.
Alternation does not replace consistent safe positioning.
takeaway: Place healthy infants on their backs for sleep.
learningObjective: Place healthy infants on their backs for sleep.

title: Car-seat sleep at home
stem: An infant falls asleep in a car seat after arriving home. What should the caregiver do?
options: Leave the infant there for the nap
Prop the seat more upright
Move the infant to a suitable firm, flat sleep surface
Add a neck pillow to support the head
why: A car seat is not the routine sleep space outside travel.
More upright positioning does not ensure a safe airway.
An approved flat sleep surface avoids positional breathing hazards.
Extra padding can introduce obstruction and entrapment risks.
takeaway: Move sleeping infants from sitting devices to a suitable sleep space.
learningObjective: Move sleeping infants from sitting devices to a suitable sleep space.

title: Crib contents
stem: A caregiver wants to cushion the crib with bumper pads and soft toys. Which advice best addresses the risk?
options: Use only thinner bumpers
Place toys at the foot of the crib
Keep padding if the baby is observed remotely
Keep the sleep space clear of soft objects and loose bedding
why: Thinner padding can still create obstruction or entrapment.
Objects can move and remain accessible during sleep.
A monitor does not prevent mechanical suffocation.
A clear sleep space reduces avoidable airway hazards.
takeaway: Keep infant sleep spaces clear of soft objects.
learningObjective: Keep infant sleep spaces clear of soft objects.

title: Adult bed transition
stem: After breastfeeding, a very tired parent expects to fall asleep while holding their newborn in bed. Which plan best reduces the immediate sleep risk?
options: Return the infant to the approved bedside bassinet
Ask an awake adult to watch while the infant stays in bed
Move to a recliner while continuing to hold the infant
Place the infant on the adult mattress away from pillows
why: A separate approved flat, firm sleep space avoids the adult-bed and caregiver-sleep hazards.
Another observer does not make a shared adult sleep surface the safest infant sleep arrangement.
Recliners create dangerous gaps and positioning if the caregiver falls asleep.
Removing pillows does not remove all adult-mattress, entrapment and bed-sharing risks.
takeaway: Plan a safe infant sleep space before caregiver sleep.
learningObjective: Plan a safe infant sleep space before caregiver sleep.

title: Sleep-product marketing
stem: A parent buys a soft infant lounger advertised as supervised sleep support. What should guide advice?
options: The number of positive reviews
Whether it meets requirements for an appropriate infant sleep space
Whether the fabric is breathable
Whether it is used only for short naps
why: Reviews do not establish sleep safety.
Product suitability must be assessed for the actual intended sleep use.
A fabric claim does not remove soft-surface and entrapment risks.
Short sleep periods can still involve airway compromise.
takeaway: Marketing terms do not establish an infant product's sleep safety.
learningObjective: Marketing terms do not establish an infant product's sleep safety.

title: Sleep after independent rolling
stem: A healthy six-month-old now rolls independently in both directions during sleep. Which caregiver statements show appropriate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: I will still place my baby on their back to start each sleep
I will use a wedge to keep my baby from turning over
I do not need to turn my baby back after independent rolling
I will add padding where my baby rolls toward the crib side
I will keep the approved crib free of loose soft objects
why: Initial back placement remains recommended even after rolling develops.
Positioning wedges introduce airway and entrapment hazards.
An infant who independently rolls does not need repeated repositioning onto the back.
Extra padding can create a suffocation hazard when the baby rolls toward it.
A clear firm sleep surface remains important as the baby becomes mobile.
takeaway: Continue initial back placement and a clear sleep space after independent rolling develops.
learningObjective: Evaluate safe-sleep teaching after an infant begins rolling independently.

title: Battery ingestion without symptoms
stem: A caregiver suspects a toddler swallowed a button battery but the child appears well. What should the nurse advise?
options: Check stools before seeking care
Wait for abdominal pain
Seek emergency assessment immediately
Offer a full meal to help passage
why: Waiting may allow severe internal injury.
Serious injury can begin before obvious symptoms.
Suspected ingestion requires time-sensitive emergency evaluation.
Feeding is not a substitute for urgent assessment.
takeaway: Suspected button-battery ingestion is urgent even without symptoms.
learningObjective: Suspected button-battery ingestion is urgent even without symptoms.

title: Battery storage
stem: A family stores spare button batteries in a low drawer beside toys. Which storage change most reliably prevents toddler access?
options: Keep batteries in their original packages in the drawer
Separate used batteries from new ones in the drawer
Put batteries in a lidded container on a reachable shelf
Place batteries in a locked cupboard beyond child access
why: Packaging alone may not prevent a child from reaching or opening it.
Both new and used batteries can cause serious ingestion injury.
A reachable lid is not a reliable barrier to a curious toddler.
Restricted access addresses the ingestion opportunity regardless of charge or packaging.
takeaway: Prevent access to both new and used button batteries.
learningObjective: Prevent access to both new and used button batteries.

title: Magnet ingestion
stem: A caregiver saw a child put small powerful magnets in their mouth, and two magnets are missing. The child has no pain. What advice is appropriate?
options: Seek immediate medical assessment
Watch for the magnets in the next stool
Offer food and monitor for abdominal discomfort
Arrange a primary-care assessment the next morning
why: Suspected magnet ingestion warrants immediate assessment because injury can develop before symptoms.
Waiting for passage can delay care while magnets attract across bowel tissue.
Food and symptom observation do not neutralize the internal magnetic hazard.
Next-day assessment may delay treatment of a potentially time-sensitive injury.
takeaway: Suspected magnet ingestion needs prompt medical assessment.
learningObjective: Suspected magnet ingestion needs prompt medical assessment.

title: Toy age mismatch
stem: A toddler repeatedly mouths objects while sharing a room with a sibling who uses a small-piece construction set. What is the best prevention plan?
options: Supervise both children while they share the construction set
Provide separate play and storage areas for the small pieces
Teach the toddler to keep construction pieces out of their mouth
Inspect the construction set for damaged pieces before play
why: Supervision helps, but ready access still permits a rapid choking event.
Physical separation addresses predictable developmental mouthing and access to small parts.
A toddler cannot consistently apply this instruction.
Undamaged small pieces can still obstruct an airway.
takeaway: Keep older children's small-part toys away from toddlers.
learningObjective: Keep older children's small-part toys away from toddlers.

title: Balloon fragments
stem: After a party, a preschooler collects broken latex balloon pieces for play. What should the caregiver do?
options: Keep the largest fragments for supervised craft work
Replace the fragments with uninflated latex balloons
Remove and discard the fragments beyond child access
Have the child play with the fragments at the table
why: Flexible fragments can conform to and obstruct the airway despite apparent size.
Uninflated balloons also present a serious choking hazard.
Removing accessible balloon material eliminates the immediate choking opportunity.
A table setting and supervision do not remove the hazard from flexible balloon pieces.
takeaway: Discard broken latex balloons where children cannot reach them.
learningObjective: Discard broken latex balloons where children cannot reach them.

title: Child poison storage
stem: Which home changes reduce accidental poisoning? Select all that apply.
options: Keep medicines in secure original containers
Store cleaners away from food access
Transfer cleaner into a familiar drink bottle
Treat child-resistant caps as one layer of protection
why: Original packaging preserves identity while secure storage restricts access.
Separation reduces mistaken ingestion.
Drink containers can encourage accidental ingestion.
Child-resistant does not mean child-proof.
takeaway: Combine secure storage with clear original packaging.
learningObjective: Combine secure storage with clear original packaging.

title: Medication visitor bag
stem: During a home visit, a toddler opens a visitor's handbag containing pill bottles. What is the priority?
options: Check whether each bottle has a child-resistant cap
Ask the visitor to watch the bag during the visit
Put the loose bottles in a nearby kitchen drawer
Move the bag to secure storage beyond the child's access
why: Caps reduce access but do not eliminate it, and checking them leaves the current access problem.
Informal watching is less reliable than secure storage when attention shifts.
An ordinary nearby drawer may remain accessible to the toddler.
Secure placement immediately removes the current ingestion opportunity.
takeaway: Include visitors' belongings in child poison prevention.
learningObjective: Include visitors' belongings in child poison prevention.

title: Unknown household ingestion
stem: A child may have swallowed a household chemical and is awake without respiratory distress. What should the caregiver do promptly?
options: Contact the poison service with the product container available
Induce vomiting before calling
Give a neutralizing household substance
Wait until symptoms identify the chemical's effect
why: Product-specific advice guides safe immediate management.
Vomiting can worsen some exposures and cause aspiration.
Improvised neutralization can create additional injury.
Waiting may lose an opportunity for effective early treatment.
takeaway: Obtain product-specific poison advice without improvised remedies.
learningObjective: Obtain product-specific poison advice without improvised remedies.

title: Child-resistant closure teaching
stem: After teaching about a child-resistant medication closure, which statement by a grandparent shows understanding?
options: I will tighten the cap and return the bottle to the bedside table
I will keep the capped bottle locked and beyond the child's reach
I will place daily doses in the organizer on the kitchen counter
I will store the capped bottle on a high open shelf
why: A child-resistant closure delays access but is not child-proof.
Secure storage remains necessary even when the cap is correctly closed.
A reachable organizer may be easier to open than the original container.
An open shelf can become accessible through climbing and lacks the locked barrier.
takeaway: Child-resistant packaging does not replace secure storage.
learningObjective: Child-resistant packaging does not replace secure storage.

title: Bath supervision
stem: A caregiver plans to leave a toddler in a shallow bath while answering the door. What is the safest plan?
options: Ask an older preschool sibling to watch
Use a bath seat and leave briefly
Take the toddler or arrange continuous capable supervision
Leave the bathroom door open
why: A young sibling cannot provide reliable rescue supervision.
A bath seat does not prevent drowning.
Continuous capable supervision addresses the immediate water risk.
An open door does not ensure timely observation or response.
takeaway: Young children need continuous capable supervision near water.
learningObjective: Young children need continuous capable supervision near water.

title: Pool flotation aid
stem: A nonswimming child wears inflatable arm bands while adults sit several metres from a pool. Which plan provides the best protection?
options: Move an adult beside the pool while keeping the arm bands
Rely on the pool lifeguard during the child's practice
Arrange swimming lessons before the next pool visit
Keep an attentive adult within reach and use a fitted approved lifejacket
why: Closer supervision helps, but arm bands are not reliable life-saving equipment.
A lifeguard does not replace the child's direct caregiver supervision.
Lessons support skills but do not protect the child during the current water exposure.
Within-reach supervision and appropriate fitted equipment provide complementary protection.
takeaway: Flotation devices do not replace close adult supervision.
learningObjective: Flotation devices do not replace close adult supervision.

title: Water-safety planning
stem: At a busy pool, one adult plans to leave while another takes over supervising a young nonswimmer. Which actions support a safe handover? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm that the second adult has explicitly accepted supervision
Ask the supervising adult to monitor messages between child checks
Check the fit of the child's approved lifejacket
Treat the nearby lifeguard as the designated replacement adult
Have the first adult remain until the second is attentive and within reach
why: An explicit transfer avoids a gap in which each adult assumes the other is responsible.
Message checking divides attention during an activity where distress can be rapid and quiet.
Correct fit supports the intended protective function.
The lifeguard supervises the pool and does not replace an agreed direct caregiver.
Responsibility should transfer only when the new supervisor is ready to provide close attention.
takeaway: Combine attentive supervision with suitable water-safety equipment.
learningObjective: Combine attentive supervision with suitable water-safety equipment.

title: Window fall prevention
stem: A toddler can climb furniture beside an open upstairs window with an insect screen. Which change best addresses the fall risk?
options: Move climbable furniture and install suitable opening restrictions
Replace the insect screen with a newer undamaged screen
Allow the child shorter periods of play in that room
Teach the child to stay away from the window
why: Reducing access and restricting the opening address the pathway to a serious fall.
An insect screen is not a fall-prevention barrier even when undamaged.
A short exposure can still permit climbing and a fall.
Teaching cannot reliably control a toddler's exploration.
takeaway: Do not rely on insect screens to prevent child falls.
learningObjective: Do not rely on insect screens to prevent child falls.

title: Cord near crib
stem: A blind cord is reachable from an infant's crib. The caregiver can move the crib immediately and arrange replacement window coverings. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Shorten the cord while leaving its loop beside the crib
Move the crib clear of cords and replace the accessible-cord covering
Tie the cord ends together above the crib mattress
Use a video monitor to watch the infant near the window
why: A remaining reachable loop can still cause strangulation.
Immediate removal of access and replacement with safer coverings address both present and continuing hazards.
Knots and joined cords can create dangerous loops rather than eliminate access.
Strangulation can be rapid and quiet; monitoring does not remove the hazard.
takeaway: Keep cords completely inaccessible from infant spaces.
learningObjective: Keep cords completely inaccessible from infant spaces.

title: Unstable furniture
stem: A child climbs a dresser to reach a toy, and the dresser tips slightly. Which change most directly corrects the furniture hazard?
options: Move heavier items into the lowest drawers
Place the preferred toys on a low nearby shelf
Anchor the dresser according to manufacturer instructions
Have an adult remain nearby during play
why: Lowering the centre of gravity may help but does not replace securing tip-prone furniture.
Removing climbing incentives is useful but does not stabilize the dresser itself.
Appropriate anchoring directly addresses the demonstrated tipping risk.
Observation cannot reliably prevent a rapid furniture tip.
takeaway: Address both furniture stability and climbing incentives.
learningObjective: Address both furniture stability and climbing incentives.

title: Home hazard prioritization
stem: During a toddler home assessment, which findings need prompt correction? Select all that apply.
options: A cleaning-cabinet latch that the child demonstrates opening
A toy battery compartment secured by an intact required screw
A cord kept inaccessible by correctly installed safety components
A visitor's medication organizer inside an open floor-level bag
A dresser anchored using the manufacturer's supplied hardware
why: A nominal latch is ineffective when this child can release it.
The intact required screw prevents ordinary child access to the battery compartment.
Correctly installed components that maintain inaccessibility are protective.
The open bag gives access to potentially toxic medication.
Proper anchoring is a protective measure against tip-over.
takeaway: Prioritize hazards with immediate access to serious injury.
learningObjective: Prioritize hazards with immediate access to serious injury.

title: CO alarm response
stem: A home-care client's carbon monoxide alarm sounds; both client and nurse have headaches. What should happen?
options: Open windows and continue assessment inside
Check every appliance before leaving
Replace the alarm battery first
Leave immediately and call emergency services from outside
why: Ventilation does not establish that remaining inside is safe.
Searching prolongs exposure to an invisible hazard.
Symptoms and an alarm should not be dismissed as a battery issue.
Evacuation stops exposure while emergency assessment is arranged.
takeaway: Leave a suspected carbon-monoxide environment immediately.
learningObjective: Leave a suspected carbon-monoxide environment immediately.

title: Generator during outage
stem: A caregiver runs a fuel-powered generator in an attached garage with the door open. What should the nurse advise?
options: Move generator operation outdoors away from openings as instructed
Close the house door and continue
Run it only while everyone is awake
Use a fan to blow fumes toward the garage door
why: Outdoor placement away from openings reduces exhaust entry.
An attached garage can still allow carbon monoxide into the home.
Wakefulness does not prevent poisoning.
A fan does not establish safe exhaust removal.
takeaway: Never operate fuel-burning generators in attached indoor spaces.
learningObjective: Never operate fuel-burning generators in attached indoor spaces.

title: Smoke alarm versus CO alarm
stem: A client with a fuel-burning furnace has a smoke alarm but no carbon-monoxide detector. Which addition provides warning of carbon monoxide?
options: Move the smoke alarm closer to the furnace
Install a certified carbon-monoxide alarm as directed
Arrange more frequent routine furnace servicing
Keep a window partly open during furnace operation
why: Relocation does not make a smoke alarm detect carbon monoxide.
A suitable CO alarm is designed to detect the otherwise imperceptible gas.
Maintenance helps prevention but does not provide ongoing detection.
An open window does not reliably prevent exposure or provide a warning.
takeaway: Use detection appropriate to the hazard.
learningObjective: Use detection appropriate to the hazard.

title: Oxygen and trip hazard
stem: A client prescribed continuous oxygen uses a walker between the chair and bathroom. Tubing crosses that route, and a shorter tube would not reach the bathroom. Which plan best addresses both needs?
options: Change to the shorter tube and keep the client near the chair
Tape the existing tube directly across the walking route
Arrange supplier-guided routing that preserves prescribed delivery
Move the chair closer to the concentrator for daytime use
why: The shorter tube would limit essential movement or interrupt prescribed oxygen.
A tube crossing the route can remain an uneven surface and become loose despite tape.
A suitable routing solution addresses the trip hazard while maintaining oxygen during necessary mobility.
Chair placement alone does not resolve the bathroom route.
takeaway: Resolve tubing hazards without compromising prescribed therapy.
learningObjective: Resolve tubing hazards without compromising prescribed therapy.

title: Oxygen supply interruption
stem: During a power outage, a home oxygen concentrator stops. The client is awake with no new distress, and a checked backup cylinder with the prescribed setup is beside the chair. What should the trained nurse do first?
options: Call the supplier to ask when power will return
Arrange a move to a neighbour whose power is working
Request emergency transport to an acute-care facility
Start the prescribed backup oxygen and verify delivery
why: The supplier can help next, but available backup should first maintain treatment.
Transporting the client is unnecessary before using the ready prescribed backup and assessing its adequacy.
Emergency help is needed if clinically indicated, but the current stable client has an immediately available support plan.
The verified backup restores prescribed delivery while ongoing assessment and outage planning proceed.
takeaway: Prepare and use a contingency plan for power-dependent care.
learningObjective: Prepare and use a contingency plan for power-dependent care.

title: Home oxygen teach-back
stem: Which statements show appropriate understanding of home oxygen safety? Select all that apply.
options: I will ask the supplier about equipment maintenance
I can turn up the flow whenever I feel anxious
I will keep ignition sources away from oxygen equipment
I will keep a plan for power or supply interruption
why: Maintenance supports reliable delivery.
Flow changes should follow the prescribed plan rather than anxiety alone.
Oxygen increases combustion risk near ignition sources.
Contingency planning supports safe ongoing therapy.
takeaway: Teach equipment reliability and contingency along with fire safety.
learningObjective: Teach equipment reliability and contingency along with fire safety.

title: Household chemical mixing
stem: A caregiver plans to mix two cleaners to improve bathroom disinfection. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Mix products that are each safe when used separately
Use one approved product according to its instructions
Add extra water after combining the cleaning products
Mix a small amount outdoors with greater ventilation
why: Separately safe products can react dangerously when combined.
Label-directed single-product use avoids unverified incompatibilities.
Dilution after mixing may not stop a hazardous reaction.
Small volume and ventilation do not establish chemical compatibility.
takeaway: Do not improvise mixtures of cleaning chemicals.
learningObjective: Do not improvise mixtures of cleaning chemicals.

title: Unlabelled cleaner at home
stem: A caregiver has decanted a known cleaner into a drinking-water bottle. What storage arrangement should replace this practice?
options: Add a handwritten cleaner label to the beverage bottle
Place the beverage bottle on a high open shelf
Keep future cleaner supplies in original labelled secure storage
Tell household members which drinking bottle contains cleaner
why: A beverage container can still be mistaken for a drink despite a handwritten label.
A high shelf does not correct the misleading container and may be reachable.
The known decanted product should be handled through its safe disposal/storage instructions; future supplies should retain original identification and secure access.
Warnings may be forgotten or not reach visitors and children.
takeaway: Never store household chemicals in beverage containers.
learningObjective: Never store household chemicals in beverage containers.

title: Home exit obstruction
stem: Boxes block the only exit route, leaving a gap too narrow for a client's walker. Which action should the nurse prioritize with the client?
options: Place emergency contact numbers beside the telephone
Arrange an additional smoke alarm near the bedroom
Schedule an emergency-evacuation practice session
Clear a continuous route wide enough for the walker
why: Contact information supports response but does not permit the client to exit.
Detection is important but does not remove the physical escape barrier.
Practice cannot safely use an exit that is currently impassable.
The demonstrated obstruction must be corrected to make emergency movement possible.
takeaway: Include accessible escape routes in home safety assessment.
learningObjective: Include accessible escape routes in home safety assessment.

title: Home emergency planning
stem: A client living alone uses a powered wheelchair and requires assistance to transfer. Their apartment is above ground level. Which proposed outage preparations are usable components of a safe plan? Select all that apply.
options: Arrange a reachable assistance network with agreed check-ins
Leave a manual wheelchair for the client to transfer into independently
Maintain compatible charged backup power as instructed
Plan to use the usual elevator when a fire alarm activates
Arrange an assessed evacuation route and trained assistance
why: An agreed reachable network can provide help when mobility or communication systems fail.
This client cannot independently perform the transfer required by that proposed backup.
Compatible maintained power supports the equipment within its limits while further help is arranged.
A normal elevator may be unsafe or unavailable during a fire; the assessed building response must guide evacuation.
The plan must match actual transfer ability and building conditions rather than assume independent escape.
takeaway: Make emergency plans fit the client's equipment and mobility needs.
learningObjective: Make emergency plans fit the client's equipment and mobility needs.

title: Threatening visitor positioning
stem: A visitor stands and makes escalating verbal threats in a small interview room. The nurse has an unobstructed route to the open door. What should the nurse do?
options: Move toward the exit and summon support
Move closer to hear the visitor's concerns
Ask the visitor to sit before continuing discussion
Remain seated and offer further reassurance
why: Using the available exit and help route reduces entrapment as the threat escalates.
Closer proximity increases exposure to sudden physical contact.
A request to sit may be part of de-escalation but should not delay securing an available safety route.
Remaining seated farther from the exit can reduce escape options if the threat increases.
takeaway: Maintain exit access when behaviour becomes threatening.
learningObjective: Maintain exit access when behaviour becomes threatening.

title: Home-visit check-in missed
stem: A lone home-care worker has missed a required check-in, and the written protocol's contact threshold has been exceeded. What should the coordinator do?
options: Send the next available worker directly to the address
Begin the defined contact and escalation sequence
Call the next scheduled client to ask about delays
Allow the usual visit-overrun period before calling
why: Sending another worker into an unknown situation may expose them to the same hazard and bypass coordinated response.
The threshold has been met; the established sequence provides accountable contact and escalation.
The next client may not know the worker's location or safety status.
The permitted threshold already accounts for when action is due.
takeaway: Follow the predetermined response to a missed worker check-in.
learningObjective: Follow the predetermined response to a missed worker check-in.

title: Escalating aggression
stem: A client clenches fists, paces and shouts while several staff prepare nonurgent care. There is no immediate need for hands-on intervention. What is the best initial response?
options: Invite several colleagues into the room to show support
Explain the complete care procedure in greater detail
Step back and use one calm lead communicator
Ask the client to sit still for a physical assessment
why: A larger group may increase the client's perceived threat and stimulation.
A long explanation may be difficult to process during escalating arousal.
Space and a single calm voice reduce competing demands while appropriate backup remains available.
A new demand for physical assessment may escalate the situation when hands-on care is not urgent.
takeaway: Adjust approach early when behaviour signals escalating risk.
learningObjective: Adjust approach early when behaviour signals escalating risk.

title: Weapon report
stem: A visitor discreetly reports seeing a weapon in another visitor's bag. The reporting person is safely beside the nurse and the suspected visitor is across the unit. What is the safest initial response under the unit's threat protocol?
options: Ask the suspected visitor whether the bag contains a weapon
Ask the suspected visitor to leave the unit immediately
Move the reporting person to another room for a detailed account
Discreetly activate the designated security response
why: Direct questioning can escalate an unverified but serious threat before trained support is ready.
A confrontation about departure may provoke danger when a weapon may be present.
The reporter is currently safe; obtaining a long account should not delay the trained response.
Prompt discreet activation enables trained threat assessment and coordinated protection.
takeaway: Use the security response for suspected weapons.
learningObjective: Use the security response for suspected weapons.

title: Violence safety handover
stem: After a client shouted and pushed a chair when approached for hygiene, staff stepped back and the client settled. Which handover entries are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Shouted and pushed a chair when two staff approached for hygiene
Intended to injure staff because the chair moved toward them
Settled after staff stepped back and one person spoke calmly
Nonurgent hygiene is paused pending the agreed reassessment
why: Specific observed behaviour and context support meaningful risk assessment.
An unverified inference about intent should not be reported as established fact.
The effective approach can guide the next team's response.
The agreed current plan clarifies what staff should do next.
takeaway: Communicate observed risks and effective responses without labels.
learningObjective: Communicate observed risks and effective responses without labels.

title: Threat after discharge
stem: A former client sends a credible threat to a nurse's work phone. What is the best response?
options: Call the former client to clarify the intended meaning
Preserve the message and activate the workplace safety process
Block the number and continue the shift assignment
Discuss the message with the nurse taking over next shift
why: Direct contact can increase exposure and should not replace the designated threat response.
Preserved evidence and formal reporting support timely risk assessment and protection.
Blocking may limit future messages but does not address the existing credible threat.
Handover alone is not a timely coordinated response to a current threat.
takeaway: Report work-related threats even after the care relationship ends.
learningObjective: Report work-related threats even after the care relationship ends.

title: A blocked doorway and safe retreat
stem: An agitated visitor blocks the main doorway. A panic alarm is within reach, and a clear side doorway leads to a staffed area. What should the nurse do next?
options: Ask the visitor to move aside for a private conversation
Remain in the room and explain the visiting policy
Activate the alarm and withdraw through the side doorway
Attempt to pass the visitor through the main doorway
why: Requesting negotiation at the blocked exit delays use of the available safe route.
A policy explanation does not address the present entrapment risk.
The available alarm and clear retreat permit help-seeking without physical confrontation.
Trying to pass a blocking person creates unnecessary contact when a safer route exists.
takeaway: Use available alarms and safe retreat routes when a threatening person blocks the main exit.
learningObjective: Select a safe retreat and support response using the actual room layout.

title: Team de-escalation roles
stem: Several staff simultaneously give different directions to an escalating client, who becomes louder and says they cannot understand. What change is most useful?
options: Rotate the speaker after each short instruction
Have each discipline explain its concern in turn
Move the whole team closer to the client
Choose one calm communicator with coordinated backup
why: Frequent changes can continue the fragmented communication.
Multiple discipline agendas may still overload the client during escalation.
Closer group presence may increase stimulation and perceived threat.
One consistent voice reduces conflicting demands while backup remains organized.
takeaway: Coordinate team roles during de-escalation.
learningObjective: Coordinate team roles during de-escalation.

title: After a threatening incident
stem: A visitor nearly strikes a nurse with a chair; no one is injured and immediate safety is restored. Which follow-up actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Wait for an injury assessment before deciding whether to report
Record objective events through the approved safety process
Review whether room layout contributed to the near miss
Remove the involved client's identity from required clinical records
Offer appropriate support to affected clients and staff
why: A serious near miss merits reporting even if no injury is identified.
Factual reporting enables risk review and an accountable response.
Layout review can identify modifiable access, object and exit hazards.
Clinical records require accurate identification and relevant care facts; privacy is protected through proper access, not inaccurate records.
The event may affect wellbeing and ongoing safety despite no physical injury.
takeaway: Learn from threats and near misses as well as injuries.
learningObjective: Learn from threats and near misses as well as injuries.

title: Care equipment as weapon risk
stem: A client recently threatened to throw objects. A nonurgent assessment is planned in a crowded room with loose equipment narrowing the exit route. What should be arranged before the assessment?
options: A clearer room with fewer loose objects and planned support
Additional staff standing inside the existing room
A verbal agreement about acceptable behaviour in the room
Placement of the equipment along the far side of the room
why: Reducing accessible hazards and preserving exit access address the identified environmental risks.
Adding people to a crowded space may worsen congestion and stimulation.
An agreement can support communication but does not remove the physical hazards.
Shifting objects within the same unsuitable space may not establish clear egress or reduce accessible hazards.
takeaway: Assess the environment when behaviour creates object-related risk.
learningObjective: Assess the environment when behaviour creates object-related risk.

title: Aggression and unmet needs
stem: A usually calm client resists scheduled hygiene while grimacing and guarding the abdomen. What should the nurse do first?
options: Offer the available PRN medication for agitation
Pause hygiene and assess the new abdominal discomfort
Reschedule hygiene for the next shift
Ask a familiar caregiver to complete the hygiene
why: Treating agitation before assessing new physical cues may mask an acute cause.
New guarding and grimacing require assessment of pain or illness before routine care proceeds.
Deferring care alone does not assess a possible developing illness.
A familiar person may reduce distress but does not evaluate the new physical findings.
takeaway: Consider physical causes when behaviour changes during care.
learningObjective: Consider physical causes when behaviour changes during care.

title: Safe visitor limit setting
stem: During urgent treatment, a visitor repeatedly reaches between staff and the client despite brief explanations. What is the best immediate response?
options: Assign one treating nurse to a longer private explanation
Ask the ill client to reassure the visitor
State a clear limit and summon appropriate team support
Move the treatment to a quieter room with the visitor
why: Removing a treating nurse for a lengthy discussion may delay urgent care while interference continues.
The client should not carry responsibility for controlling an interfering visitor.
A clear boundary and support protect the team's ability to continue urgent care.
Relocation may delay treatment and may carry the same interference into another room.
takeaway: Set clear behaviour limits that protect necessary care.
learningObjective: Set clear behaviour limits that protect necessary care.

title: Nonjudgmental risk assessment
stem: A newly admitted client with a mental-health diagnosis is calm. Staff have no reliable history of threatening behaviour or known triggers. What should guide the safety plan?
options: Use the observation level commonly associated with the diagnosis
Base the plan on the client's calm arrival presentation
Repeat the precautions used at the previous admission
Assess current behaviour, relevant history and environmental risks
why: A diagnosis may inform clinical care but does not establish an individual violence risk level.
Current calm behaviour is useful evidence but does not replace relevant history and context.
Previous precautions may no longer match current risks and must be reviewed.
Individual evidence avoids both stereotyping and false reassurance.
takeaway: Base safety measures on individual evidence rather than diagnostic labels.
learningObjective: Base safety measures on individual evidence rather than diagnostic labels.

title: Psychological safety to report
stem: A novice nurse identifies that a medication was nearly given to the wrong client; it was stopped before administration. Which leadership responses support a useful safety review? Select all that apply.
options: Check the immediate client implications and acknowledge the report
Delay formal reporting until a harmful outcome is confirmed
Review the identification process and contributing conditions
Arrange focused learning based on the review findings
Require full medication retraining before reviewing the sequence
why: Current impact should be verified, and constructive acknowledgement supports prompt hazard reporting.
Near misses can reveal important risks even when injury is prevented.
Reviewing the sequence can identify both individual and system contributors.
Education should address demonstrated needs rather than assume the cause.
Broad retraining before understanding the event may not address the actual contributors.
takeaway: Make it possible for staff to report hazards early.
learningObjective: Make it possible for staff to report hazards early.

title: Pet interference in home care
stem: A large dog repeatedly jumps at a home-care nurse preparing a sterile procedure. What should be arranged before supplies are opened?
options: Have the client hold the dog by the collar
Separate the dog securely from the treatment area
Place the sterile tray on the highest available table
Ask a second worker to distract the dog nearby
why: A collar hold may fail with a sudden movement during the procedure.
Reliable environmental separation prevents interference and supports safe sterile preparation.
Tray height does not prevent jumping into the nurse or treatment field.
Distraction may lapse and does not create a dependable barrier.
takeaway: Control environmental interference before invasive home care.
learningObjective: Control environmental interference before invasive home care.

title: Smoking during home visit
stem: A client lights a cigarette beside operating home oxygen equipment during a nurse's visit. There is no fire yet. What is the priority?
options: Document the smoking and request a supplier review
Open the nearby windows to disperse oxygen
Ask the client to extinguish it while maintaining safe distance
Disconnect the oxygen tubing from the client
why: Future review does not remove the current ignition source.
Ventilation does not make a lit cigarette near oxygen safe.
A clear request to extinguish the ignition source addresses immediate danger; maintain distance and summon help if needed rather than physically confronting the client.
Disconnection alone does not remove the lit ignition source or oxygen-enriched materials and may interrupt needed treatment.
takeaway: Act immediately on ignition sources near oxygen.
learningObjective: Act immediately on ignition sources near oxygen.

title: Emergency-access information
stem: Emergency crews previously had difficulty locating a home-care client because the address marker was missing and access is through a side entrance. Which plan best prevents another delay?
options: Explain the route to the nurse assigned next week
Describe the house colour to the client's family
Place access instructions in the indoor care binder
Correct the address marker and record authorized responder access details
why: One nurse's knowledge may not be available to emergency responders.
House colour can be ambiguous and family may not be present during an emergency.
An indoor binder cannot guide responders before they reach the client.
Visible identification and accessible authorized directions support timely location and entry.
takeaway: Make emergency access instructions clear and available to responders.
learningObjective: Make emergency access instructions clear and available to responders.

title: Medication disposal at home
stem: A family finds unused medicines accessible to children after a relative's treatment changes. What is appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Secure the medicines while arranging approved disposal
Keep them for relatives who report similar symptoms
Use the pharmacy or locally approved medication-return pathway
Put the intact tablets in the household garbage
why: Restricted access protects children while the disposal route is arranged.
A medicine prescribed for another person may be inappropriate or harmful.
An approved return route supports safe handling of unwanted medicines.
Accessible discarded medicine can expose children, animals or others; follow local approved return advice.
takeaway: Secure unwanted medicines and use an approved disposal pathway.
learningObjective: Secure unwanted medicines and use an approved disposal pathway.

title: Insulin pen mix-up
stem: Two clients use the same insulin product. A nurse proposes using one client's pen for the other after changing the needle. What should happen?
options: Use the pen if the dose is identical
Keep each pen for its assigned individual only
Disinfect the pen casing before sharing
Share only while a replacement pen is ordered
why: Matching medicine and dose do not remove bloodborne contamination risk.
A pen can become internally contaminated and must not be shared.
Surface cleaning cannot disinfect the internal cartridge.
A temporary shortage does not make shared use safe.
takeaway: Insulin pens are for one person, even with a new needle.
learningObjective: Insulin pens are for one person, even with a new needle.

title: Fingerstick device sharing
stem: A clinic changes lancets in a reusable fingerstick device between clients. Which feature explains why the device must still not be shared?
options: Variation in clients' test-strip calibration
Differences in clients' skin thickness
Possible retained blood inside the reusable device
The adjustable depth of the lancet setting
why: Test-strip calibration concerns the meter system rather than the cross-person puncture-device hazard.
Skin thickness may affect sampling technique but is not the principal infection mechanism.
Changing the lancet does not remove blood contamination that can remain within the device.
Depth adjustment affects puncture depth and does not make shared use infection-safe.
takeaway: Never share a fingerstick device between people.
learningObjective: Never share a fingerstick device between people.

title: Glucose meter selection
stem: A clinic must select a glucose meter for use with several clients. Which device is suitable?
options: A personal meter fitted with a disposable external cover
A personal meter with a smooth easy-clean casing
A meter marketed with an antimicrobial outer surface
A professional shared-use meter with validated disinfection instructions
why: A cover does not establish that the device is designed or validated for multi-client processing.
An easy-clean exterior does not establish safe shared-use design.
An antimicrobial surface claim does not replace a validated process for the whole device.
Shared-use design and validated between-client processing support appropriate selection.
takeaway: Shared glucose monitoring requires an appropriate device and validated processing.
learningObjective: Shared glucose monitoring requires an appropriate device and validated processing.

title: Glucose round workflow
stem: A nurse uses a professional shared glucose meter for a morning round. Which practices reduce cross-contamination? Select all that apply.
options: Clean hands and use fresh gloves for each client
Carry unused strips and the used meter in one uniform pocket
Process the meter after each client using its instructions
Keep clean strips separate from equipment awaiting processing
Disinfect the meter when the whole round is complete
why: Fresh gloves and hand hygiene reduce carryover of blood contamination.
Co-storage can contaminate clean supplies through contact with used equipment.
Between-client processing reduces transmission through a shared device.
Separation protects supplies intended for subsequent clients.
End-of-round processing permits intervening clients to contact a contaminated device.
takeaway: Organize glucose testing to separate clean supplies from blood exposure.
learningObjective: Organize glucose testing to separate clean supplies from blood exposure.

title: Contaminated medication cart
stem: After examining a bleeding wound, a nurse touches the shared medication-cart handle with used gloves. Which correction addresses the contamination before the round continues?
options: Remove gloves, clean hands and disinfect the handle appropriately
Change gloves and add the handle to scheduled cart cleaning
Disinfect the handle with the current gloves and continue
Assign the cart to that client for the rest of the shift
why: Both contaminated hands/gloves and the shared touch surface require correction.
Fresh gloves can be contaminated again by the untreated handle before scheduled cleaning.
Continuing with the contaminated gloves can recontaminate the cleaned surface or supplies.
Changing the cart assignment does not clean the contaminated hands or handle.
takeaway: Address both contaminated hands and surfaces after a workflow breach.
learningObjective: Address both contaminated hands and surfaces after a workflow breach.

title: Shared vial at bedside
stem: A multidose vial intended for several clients has entered one client's immediate treatment area. Which plan follows injection-safety guidance?
options: Disinfect the stopper and return it to shared stock
Dedicate it to this client or dispose of it under policy
Return it to shared stock if its cap remained in place
Use it for several clients within a shorter storage period
why: Stopper disinfection does not reverse the implications of treatment-area exposure for shared use.
A multidose vial entering an immediate treatment area should be dedicated to one client; discard when required or sterility is uncertain.
A cap does not establish that the vial can return to multi-client handling after exposure to the treatment area.
A shorter use period does not correct the cross-client contamination risk.
takeaway: Protect shared injectable supplies from patient-treatment-area contamination.
learningObjective: Protect shared injectable supplies from patient-treatment-area contamination.

title: Leftovers left overnight
stem: An older adult plans to eat cooked chicken left on the counter overnight because it smells normal. What should the nurse advise?
options: Reheat until it smells freshly cooked
Taste a small portion before deciding
Discard food held unsafely; smell cannot establish safety
Refrigerate it now and eat it tomorrow
why: Reheating does not reliably correct every hazard from prolonged unsafe storage.
Tasting can expose the person to contaminated food.
Pathogens or toxins may be present without an abnormal smell.
Late refrigeration does not reverse prior microbial growth.
takeaway: Do not judge food safety by smell after unsafe storage.
learningObjective: Do not judge food safety by smell after unsafe storage.

title: Raw and ready-to-eat food
stem: During a home visit, raw poultry juice is dripping onto washed salad in the refrigerator. What should the nurse advise?
options: Rinse the salad and move the poultry to a lower shelf
Discard the wet leaves and serve the rest of the salad
Lower the refrigerator temperature to chill both foods rapidly
Discard the salad and store raw poultry below ready-to-eat food
why: Rinsing cannot reliably make contaminated ready-to-eat salad safe.
Contamination may extend beyond the visibly wet leaves.
Refrigeration does not remove organisms transferred onto food that will not be cooked.
Discarding exposed salad and correcting raw-food placement address the current contamination and recurrence.
takeaway: Keep raw animal-food juices away from ready-to-eat foods.
learningObjective: Keep raw animal-food juices away from ready-to-eat foods.

title: Food-safety teaching
stem: An older adult describes preparing chicken and a ready-to-eat salad. Which steps support food safety? Select all that apply.
options: Cut salad vegetables on the board used for raw chicken
Wash hands after handling raw chicken before salad preparation
Divide cooked leftovers into suitable containers for prompt refrigeration
Return cooked chicken to the plate that held it raw
Clean and disinfect preparation surfaces as directed between tasks
why: The raw-chicken board can transfer organisms onto food that will not be cooked.
Handwashing interrupts transfer from raw poultry to ready-to-eat ingredients.
Appropriate divided storage and prompt cooling limit growth in leftovers.
The raw-food plate can recontaminate the cooked chicken.
Surface processing between incompatible tasks helps prevent cross-contamination.
takeaway: Control food contamination and storage conditions together.
learningObjective: Control food contamination and storage conditions together.

title: Dietary allergen mismatch
stem: A client with a documented severe milk-protein allergy receives a tray marked lactose-free. Which verification should occur before serving it?
options: Confirm the tray matches the lactose-free diet code
Check ingredients for milk protein and obtain a suitable tray
Request the kitchen's usual lactose-free dairy substitution
Review the tray's total carbohydrate information
why: The diet code addresses lactose but may not exclude allergenic milk protein.
Milk-protein allergy differs from lactose intolerance; ingredient verification is needed before exposure.
Lactose-free dairy can still contain milk proteins.
Carbohydrate information does not establish absence of milk allergens.
takeaway: Verify the actual allergen rather than relying on a related dietary label.
learningObjective: Verify the actual allergen rather than relying on a related dietary label.

title: Damp central-line dressing
stem: A client's central-line dressing is saturated after sweating; the scheduled change is tomorrow. The nurse is competent and authorized for dressing care. What should happen now?
options: Wait until tomorrow's scheduled dressing change
Secure the existing dressing with an extra tape border
Replace the dressing using the approved aseptic procedure
Reinforce the covering with another transparent dressing
why: A compromised damp dressing needs replacement before the routine interval.
Additional tape does not restore a saturated barrier.
Aseptic replacement restores appropriate site protection.
An outer dressing traps the damp material rather than correcting the compromised covering.
takeaway: Replace compromised vascular-access dressings rather than waiting for routine timing.
learningObjective: Replace compromised vascular-access dressings rather than waiting for routine timing.

title: Dressing choice for an oozing site
stem: A newly inserted vascular catheter site continues to ooze small amounts of blood beneath a transparent dressing. The competent, authorized nurse follows the device protocol. Which covering is preferred while oozing continues?
options: A fresh transparent semipermeable film
A chlorhexidine-impregnated transparent dressing
The current intact film until the routine change time
An appropriate sterile gauze dressing
why: A nonabsorbent film is less suitable when blood continues to collect.
Antimicrobial properties do not replace the need to manage active oozing with an appropriate absorbent covering.
The oozing requires reassessment and appropriate covering rather than waiting for the routine interval.
Sterile gauze provides absorbency while protecting the insertion site and allowing planned reassessment.
takeaway: Select the catheter dressing for the actual site condition.
learningObjective: Select the catheter dressing for the actual site condition.

title: Access-port preparation
stem: After the required scrub of a vascular connector, the antiseptic is still wet. The product instructions require air drying before access. What should the nurse do?
options: Allow the connector to air dry before attaching the syringe
Wipe away excess antiseptic using sterile gauze
Attach the sterile syringe while the connector remains wet
Scrub again using a different available antiseptic
why: Completion of the specified application and drying process supports aseptic access.
Wiping can remove the antiseptic before its intended process is complete.
Visible antiseptic does not establish that the required drying step is finished.
Changing products does not resolve the incomplete drying process and can introduce incompatibility.
takeaway: Complete connector antisepsis according to product and device instructions.
learningObjective: Complete connector antisepsis according to product and device instructions.

title: Vascular-device prevention
stem: A stable client has changed to oral treatment, with no anticipated intravenous need. A peripheral catheter remains. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm that no clinical indication for the catheter remains
Maintain the saline lock until the discharge day
Assess the site and remove the catheter when authorized
Document the site findings and resulting device plan
why: Necessity review confirms whether invasive access continues to offer benefit.
Routine retention after the indication ends adds unnecessary catheter exposure.
Removal of unnecessary access and site assessment reduce avoidable device risk.
Clear documentation supports follow-through and ongoing site care.
takeaway: Remove invasive devices when their indication has ended and removal is authorized.
learningObjective: Remove invasive devices when their indication has ended and removal is authorized.

title: Line protection during bathing
stem: A client with a vascular catheter is permitted to shower under the device protocol. Which protection should the nurse arrange?
options: Cover the insertion dressing while leaving connections exposed
Use an approved impermeable cover for the site and connections
Disconnect the infusion and leave the capped connector exposed
Plan a new dressing immediately after the shower
why: Water can reach unprotected connecting components even if the insertion dressing is covered.
The approved method should protect both the site and components from water exposure.
A capped connector still requires appropriate protection from shower contamination.
A later dressing change does not prevent contamination during the shower.
takeaway: Protect catheter sites and connections from water exposure.
learningObjective: Protect catheter sites and connections from water exposure.

title: Two wound-care tasks
stem: One client needs care of a clean surgical incision and a heavily draining contaminated wound. Both care kits require a cleansing basin. Which preparation best limits transfer between sites?
options: Prepare the draining wound first and reserve its basin for the incision
Prepare the incision first and return to it after draining-wound cleansing
Prepare separate kits and complete the incision before the draining wound
Prepare a common basin with enough solution to cover both dressings
why: A basin used for the contaminated wound should not be reused for the cleaner incision.
Returning to the cleaner site after contaminated care creates an avoidable need for a complete aseptic reset.
Separate supplies and cleaner-to-more-contaminated sequencing reduce transfer opportunities; hand hygiene and appropriate glove changes remain necessary.
A shared basin can become a route for organisms between separate wounds.
takeaway: Prevent transfer from contaminated wounds to cleaner sites.
learningObjective: Prevent transfer from contaminated wounds to cleaner sites.

title: Terminal cleaning coordination
stem: A client with infectious diarrhoea transfers out and another client awaits the bed. Which finding establishes environmental readiness?
options: Fresh bed linen and a clean gown are in place
The bed rails have been wiped with disinfectant
The room has stood vacant for a routine interval
The required terminal-cleaning and equipment checklist is complete
why: Fresh linen does not establish processing of contaminated environmental surfaces.
Bed rails are only part of the equipment and room requiring processing.
Waiting does not remove persistent surface contamination.
Completion of the required room and equipment process provides the relevant readiness evidence.
takeaway: Confirm environmental readiness before assigning the next client.
learningObjective: Confirm environmental readiness before assigning the next client.

title: Spore-targeted cleaning
stem: A room used by a client with C. difficile requires disinfection. Which compatible approved product label should guide selection?
options: A sporicidal claim with the specified application instructions
A general bactericidal claim for routine surfaces
An alcohol-based surface-cleaning claim
A neutral detergent claim for visible soil
why: C. difficile spores require an appropriately labelled sporicidal process used as instructed.
A general bactericidal claim does not establish activity against spores.
Alcohol-based cleaning does not by itself establish sporicidal activity.
Detergent helps remove soil but is not equivalent to the required disinfection.
takeaway: Match environmental disinfectant activity to the organism and task.
learningObjective: Match environmental disinfectant activity to the organism and task.

title: Disinfection verification
stem: A cleaning audit identifies the following practices. Which require correction? Select all that apply.
options: Removing visible soil before the disinfection step as instructed
Wiping the surface dry immediately after disinfectant application
Checking the equipment manufacturer's product compatibility list
Signing the cleaning log before the surface process is finished
Keeping the surface wet for the labelled contact period
why: Required soil removal supports the subsequent disinfecting process.
Immediate drying can shorten the required contact time and reduce effectiveness.
Compatibility checking helps avoid equipment damage and ineffective processing.
Premature sign-off inaccurately records completion and can release equipment before readiness.
Maintaining the stated contact period follows the validated process.
takeaway: Audit the disinfection process using its actual technical requirements.
learningObjective: Audit the disinfection process using its actual technical requirements.

title: Shared touchscreen contact
stem: A mobile touchscreen is handled during direct care in several rooms. Which plan best controls its between-client contamination risk?
options: Apply a disposable cover and replace it at the end of the day
Use compatible between-client processing and appropriate hand hygiene
Clean the screen after the last room on each shift
Provide a dedicated stylus that travels with the screen
why: A contaminated cover can transfer organisms during intervening uses.
Compatible processing at indicated transitions and hand hygiene address device and hand transfer.
End-of-shift cleaning permits cross-client transfer during the shift.
A shared stylus can itself become contaminated and does not eliminate processing needs.
takeaway: Include shared digital equipment in routine infection-control planning.
learningObjective: Include shared digital equipment in routine infection-control planning.

title: Transport stretcher turnover
stem: A stretcher returns after transporting a client with draining wounds. Which turnover process is needed before its next use?
