options: Replace the linen and spot-clean visible soil
Process the mattress and retain clean-looking linen
Replace linen and process exposed equipment according to protocol
Place a fresh disposable sheet over the used surface
why: Visible-soil cleaning alone may not complete required surface disinfection.
Used linen can carry contamination despite appearing clean.
Both linen replacement and appropriate equipment processing interrupt transfer.
An outer sheet does not establish cleaning of the underlying exposed equipment.
takeaway: Process transport equipment between clients according to exposure.
learningObjective: Process transport equipment between clients according to exposure.

title: Coughing visitor in oncology
stem: A visitor with new cough and fever wants an elective social visit beside an immunocompromised client. Current screening guidance advises symptomatic visitors to defer. What is best?
options: Provide a procedure mask for a brief bedside visit
Arrange a visit from across the client's room
Schedule the visit after the visitor takes an antipyretic
Defer the in-person visit and arrange remote contact
why: Masking reduces some exposure but does not replace the stated screening guidance for this elective visit.
Room distance does not eliminate exposure in a shared indoor space.
Reducing fever does not establish that the infectious risk has resolved.
Deferral follows the identified guidance while remote contact maintains social support.
takeaway: Adapt visits when symptoms create risk for a vulnerable client.
learningObjective: Adapt visits when symptoms create risk for a vulnerable client.

title: Airborne-room alarm
stem: An airborne-isolation room's pressure alarm signals airflow failure. The infectious client is stable inside, and no replacement room has yet been verified. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep the door closed and activate the facilities/IPAC response
Move the client to the nearest available private room
Increase airflow using a portable floor fan
Reset the alarm after checking that the door is shut
why: Maintaining containment while obtaining coordinated engineering and placement advice addresses the failed control.
A nearby private room may not provide the needed airborne containment.
An unapproved fan may disrupt airflow and spread contaminated air.
A closed door check does not establish restored pressure; resetting alone may hide the ongoing fault.
takeaway: Treat failure of isolation engineering controls as a safety problem.
learningObjective: Treat failure of isolation engineering controls as a safety problem.

title: Isolation response readiness
stem: A unit will receive a client requiring airborne precautions. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the designated room and respiratory protection pathway
Use a positive-pressure protective room as an interchangeable substitute
Notify receiving staff of the needed precautions
Arrange essential supplies to reduce avoidable traffic
why: Placement and protection should be ready before exposure occurs.
Positive pressure can push room air outward and is not equivalent containment.
Advance communication supports consistent precautions.
Preparation reduces unnecessary entry and exit.
takeaway: Prepare the environment and team before receiving an airborne-risk client.
learningObjective: Prepare the environment and team before receiving an airborne-risk client.

title: Unsafe doffing sequence observed
stem: During glove removal, a colleague contaminates a bare wrist and is about to resume care. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the colleague to put on fresh gloves
Prompt appropriate cleaning of the contaminated skin now
Report the technique breach after the current task
Arrange a PPE demonstration at the next team huddle
why: Covering the area does not remove the contamination and may spread it during further care.
Immediate cleaning interrupts the present transfer risk; focused private feedback can follow.
Later reporting does not correct the contamination before further contact.
Education can help prevent recurrence but does not first remove the current contamination.
takeaway: Correct observed contamination immediately and use it for focused learning.
learningObjective: Correct observed contamination immediately and use it for focused learning.

title: Specimen requisition contamination
stem: An intact urine container is securely closed, but its requisition is placed in the specimen compartment of a transport bag with a separate document pouch. How should the nurse package it?
options: Wrap the requisition around the closed container
Place the whole package inside a second specimen bag
Move the requisition into the separate document pouch
Tape a photocopy of the requisition to the outer bag
why: Paper around the container remains in the compartment where leakage could occur.
An extra bag does not separate clean paperwork from the specimen compartment.
The designated separate pouch protects paperwork and supports clean receiving handling.
An exterior photocopy does not correct placement of the original paper and may not meet the approved transport process.
takeaway: Protect accompanying paperwork from specimen contamination.
learningObjective: Protect accompanying paperwork from specimen contamination.

title: Body-fluid spill on walkway
stem: A fresh blood spill crosses a busy walkway. The affected client is stable. The nurse has no spill PPE immediately available, and a trained cleanup team is being contacted. What should happen now?
options: Place a warning sign beside the spill and resume care
Cover the blood with absorbent material and leave
Begin wiping the spill with the available dry towels
Restrict the route until appropriately protected cleanup occurs
why: A sign warns but may not reliably keep people from a busy contaminated route.
Covering can conceal the hazard and does not maintain accountable access control.
Cleanup should use the required protection and process.
Immediate route control prevents further contact and slips while trained cleanup is arranged.
takeaway: Isolate a contaminated spill area until safe cleanup is complete.
learningObjective: Isolate a contaminated spill area until safe cleanup is complete.

title: Blood exposure with intact skin
stem: Blood splashes onto a nurse's bare forearm. The skin appears intact, but it has not yet been closely inspected. What should the nurse do first?
options: Wash the exposed skin promptly with soap and water
Apply alcohol hand rub over the affected forearm
Call occupational health before touching the exposed area
Check the source client's infection status in the record
why: Prompt washing removes contamination; then inspect skin integrity and obtain proportionate exposure guidance if needed.
Soap and water is appropriate for removing visible blood contamination.
Exposure guidance is important when indicated but should not delay immediate washing.
Source information does not replace immediate cleaning and assessment of the exposure route.
takeaway: Clean contamination promptly and assess the actual exposure route.
learningObjective: Clean contamination promptly and assess the actual exposure route.

title: Sterile supply checks
stem: Before selecting a sterile invasive-procedure kit, the nurse inspects several packages. Which findings require replacing the affected kit? Select all that apply.
options: The wrapper is damp where liquid reached it
The external process indicator shows its expected colour change
The required contents match the planned procedure
The printed expiry date has passed under the facility's dating policy
The sealed wrapper is dry and its integrity is intact
why: Moisture can compromise the sterile barrier.
Expected external indicator change is part of checking processing but is not by itself a reason to discard an otherwise suitable package.
Correct contents establish suitability rather than a reason for replacement.
A package beyond the applicable dated limit should not be selected for use.
An intact dry barrier is a required protective finding, considered with the other sterility checks.
takeaway: Verify both sterility and procedural suitability before opening supplies.
learningObjective: Verify both sterility and procedural suitability before opening supplies.

title: Newborn identification mismatch
stem: A newborn's identification band loosens and comes off before transfer back to the parent. The unit has an approved parent–infant band-replacement process. What should the nurse use to re-establish identification?
options: The cot card and the baby's current bed location
The documented matched identifiers and approved replacement checks
Recognition by the nurse assigned throughout the shift
The parent's recognition of the infant's appearance
why: Location and a cot card are not a sufficient replacement for the approved identity linkage.
The established matching and replacement process restores a traceable parent–infant identity link.
Staff recognition can support care but should not replace formal newborn identification checks.
Parent recognition is valuable but is not the complete approved band-replacement process.
takeaway: Resolve newborn identification discrepancies before transfer or feeding.
learningObjective: Resolve newborn identification discrepancies before transfer or feeding.

title: Similar names in clinic
stem: Two clients with similar names await the same procedure. Which check best prevents wrong-client care?
options: Ask whether the person is here for the planned procedure
Match the person to the scheduled appointment time
Ask for required identifiers and match them to the order
Read the expected name aloud and ask for agreement
why: Both clients can truthfully confirm the same procedure.
Appointment timing can change and is not a personal identifier.
Open-ended identifiers checked against the order establish the correct person-to-record link.
A leading yes/no name question can be misheard or agreed to mistakenly.
takeaway: Use personal identifiers when shared names and procedures create confusion.
learningObjective: Use personal identifiers when shared names and procedures create confusion.

title: Procedure timeout concern
stem: Before an elective procedure, the surgeon says a site discrepancy was corrected verbally. The team cannot see a corroborating record and one member remains uncertain. What should happen?
options: Proceed using the surgeon's verbal assurance
Ask the family which side they recall discussing
Use the site printed on the original booking list
Repeat the team verification after the records are reconciled
why: An unresolved shared verification gap remains despite an individual assurance.
Family recollection may contribute information but does not complete the team's required reconciliation.
The booking record could be the source of the original discrepancy.
Visible, shared verification of the reconciled plan resolves the uncertainty before the elective procedure.
takeaway: A safety pause must produce a verified shared plan.
learningObjective: A safety pause must produce a verified shared plan.

title: Wrong texture tray
stem: A client's current swallowing plan specifies a modified food texture. A regular tray arrives and the client is hungry. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A replacement meal matching the assessed texture plan
Smaller pieces cut from the regular-texture meal
Thickened fluid alongside the regular-texture food
The softest-looking items from the regular tray
why: The actual food must meet the specified assessed texture standard before feeding.
Smaller pieces do not necessarily achieve the prescribed texture and consistency.
Changing liquid consistency does not correct unsuitable solid food texture.
Visual softness does not reliably establish compliance with the assessed texture requirement.
takeaway: Match delivered food with the current swallowing plan.
learningObjective: Match delivered food with the current swallowing plan.

title: Enteral-line connection check
stem: After transfer, an enteral-only feeding connector does not fit the available tubing. Several infusion lines are also present. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use a general adapter to join the available tubing
Trace the feeding route from client to source
Obtain compatible enteral-specific components
Connect the feeding tube to the unused infusion extension
Verify the feeding prescription and setup before restart
why: A generic adapter can defeat route-specific protection and permit a dangerous misconnection.
Route tracing confirms the intended system before connection.
Compatible enteral components preserve the intended route-specific safety design.
Infusion tubing is not an appropriate substitute for the enteral route.
The correct route and equipment must also match the prescribed treatment.
takeaway: Verify both route and treatment before restarting enteral delivery.
learningObjective: Verify both route and treatment before restarting enteral delivery.

title: Transfer-board support
stem: A client with paraplegia is ready for their established assisted transfer-board transfer. Their strength and sitting balance are unchanged. After a mattress replacement, the board rests firmly on the wheelchair but rocks on the rounded mattress edge. The client has not moved onto the board. What should the nurse do next?
options: Ask a second worker to hold the mattress end during transfer
Reposition the equipment to obtain firm support at both ends
Place a folded towel beneath the board at the mattress edge
Advance the chair end farther beneath the client before transfer
why: A worker holding the rocking end does not establish a stable supporting surface for the loaded board.
Both ends must rest firmly on suitable surfaces before the client loads the board. The changed mattress requires correction of the setup even though the client's abilities are unchanged.
Improvised padding may shift or compress and does not reliably correct the unstable support.
Moving more board toward the wheelchair can further reduce support at the mattress end; the entire placement must be corrected.
takeaway: Confirm firm support at both ends of a transfer board before loading it.
learningObjective: Recognize when a changed support surface makes an established transfer-board setup unsafe.

title: Worn walking-aid tips
stem: A client's walking aid slips on a dry floor and its rubber tips are visibly worn. What should be arranged before the next walk?
options: Closer staff assistance while using the same aid
Restriction of the same aid to short walks in the room
Appropriate replacement tips or a checked alternative aid
Nonslip household tape wrapped around the worn tips
why: Closer assistance does not restore the equipment's lost traction.
A short walk still loads the slipping tips.
A suitable repair or checked alternative corrects the observed mechanical fault.
An improvised material may detach or alter safe contact under load.
takeaway: Inspect and replace worn mobility-aid components.
learningObjective: Inspect and replace worn mobility-aid components.

title: Bed height after care
stem: After wound care, a bed remains at treatment height. The client usually transfers independently but is now mildly weak. What should the nurse do before leaving?
options: Lower the bed to its floor-level setting
Activate the bed alarm at the current height
Use the client's usual independent-transfer plan
Set a suitable exit height and assess the current transfer
why: The lowest possible setting may make standing difficult; exit height should match the client.
An alarm does not correct an unsafe height or establish current transfer ability.
New weakness may change the assistance needed from baseline.
Appropriate height and present performance together determine a safe transfer plan.
takeaway: Restore the environment to match the client's current mobility needs.
learningObjective: Restore the environment to match the client's current mobility needs.

title: Concealed wet floor
stem: A client with an unsteady gait needs to reach the bathroom. The usual route is damp from cleaning and a dry alternative is available. Which action best controls the immediate slip risk?
options: Arrange assisted access along the dry alternative route
Escort the client slowly across the damp route
Place a warning sign beside the damp route
Provide nonslip footwear for the usual route
why: A dry accessible route removes the current floor hazard while meeting the client's need for assistance.
Slow walking does not remove the slippery surface.
A warning does not provide the client a safe route to the bathroom.
Footwear helps traction but does not make avoidable exposure to a wet route the best choice.
takeaway: Control access to hazards while preserving a safe alternate route.
learningObjective: Control access to hazards while preserving a safe alternate route.

title: Restraint use and staffing
stem: A calm resident walks purposefully around the unit and has no immediate danger or treatment interference. During a staffing shortage, a colleague proposes restraint to reduce observation needs. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the prescriber for a temporary restraint order
Ask family to agree to the proposed restraint
Assess walking needs and escalate staffing or supervision alternatives
Administer the available PRN medication for agitation
why: An order does not establish that restraint is clinically necessary in the stated circumstances.
Agreement does not replace a clinical indication and consideration of alternatives.
The response should meet the resident's actual needs and address resource limits through appropriate support.
The resident is calm; medication for agitation does not address the staffing problem.
takeaway: Resource pressure does not by itself justify restricting a client.
learningObjective: Resource pressure does not by itself justify restricting a client.

title: Emergency drill learning
stem: A power-failure drill revealed that staff could not access backup batteries. Which findings demonstrate that the correction is effective? Select all that apply.
options: An email describing the intended storage change has been sent
Staff can retrieve the approved batteries during a repeat timed check
The issue is listed for the next annual drill agenda
Staff demonstrate the trained battery connection procedure
A named owner verifies that access and charging checks are maintained
why: Information delivery alone does not establish usable access.
A practical repeat check tests whether the original retrieval barrier is corrected.
Listing future discussion does not demonstrate present readiness.
Retrieval must be paired with competent use of the backup.
Maintained ownership and checks support sustained readiness beyond the single drill.
takeaway: Emergency exercises should produce verified practical corrections.
learningObjective: Emergency exercises should produce verified practical corrections.

title: Evacuation assistance mismatch
stem: A resident now requires a mechanical lift, but the evacuation record still lists independent walking. What should be done now?
options: Add a routine mobility note to the daily care chart
Tell the usual day-shift nurse about the change
Update the evacuation assistance and equipment plan
Assign a wheelchair during the next scheduled drill
why: A routine note may not update the specific emergency information responders use.
One colleague's knowledge does not establish an accessible current emergency plan.
The emergency plan must reflect present dependence and an assessed feasible evacuation method.
A later drill leaves the current plan unsafe and a wheelchair alone may not meet transfer needs.
takeaway: Update emergency plans when functional assistance needs change.
learningObjective: Update emergency plans when functional assistance needs change.

title: Latex exposure from visitors
stem: A client with a severe latex allergy receives latex balloons from visitors. The nurse has already selected nonlatex care supplies. What next?
options: Allow balloons because they are not medical supplies
Keep them near the window rather than the bed
Ask the client to report symptoms before removal
Remove the exposure and explain suitable alternatives
why: Environmental latex sources can still create exposure.
Room placement does not reliably eliminate the risk.
Waiting permits avoidable allergen contact.
The prevention plan should include nonclinical items brought into the room.
takeaway: Include visitor items when managing environmental allergens.
learningObjective: Include visitor items when managing environmental allergens.

title: Shared personal grooming tool
stem: Two residents share an electric razor and one has small shaving cuts. Which plan best controls possible blood exposure?
options: Use individual razors or the device's validated shared-use process
Rinse the cutting head between the two residents
Change the detachable head and continue sharing the body
Wipe the outer casing after removing visible hair
why: Individual use avoids transfer, while any permitted reuse must follow the actual device's validated processing instructions.
A quick rinse may leave blood contamination within cutting components.
A head change alone does not establish that the remaining device has been processed safely for another resident.
Outer-surface cleaning may not process internal or cutting parts exposed to blood.
takeaway: Consider blood contamination when sharing personal-care equipment.
learningObjective: Consider blood contamination when sharing personal-care equipment.

title: Clean uniform after splash
stem: A nurse's uniform becomes visibly contaminated with body fluid before care of another client. What should happen?
options: Spot-clean the affected fabric with detergent
Change the contaminated clothing and clean exposed skin
Cover the affected area with a clean protective gown
Complete the current round and change afterward
why: Spot treatment during wear does not establish appropriate clothing decontamination.
Removing contaminated clothing through the approved process and addressing skin limits onward contact.
An outer covering leaves the contaminated clothing in place and can be displaced.
Continuing rounds can carry contamination to other care environments.
takeaway: Remove contaminated clothing from ongoing clinical contact.
learningObjective: Remove contaminated clothing from ongoing clinical contact.

title: Infection precautions and mobility
stem: A stable client on contact precautions has covered wound drainage and can perform hand hygiene. The care plan includes walking, and local guidance permits a planned route. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on a route and timing consistent with the precautions plan
Join the shared recreation group instead of the planned walk
Check drainage containment and perform hand hygiene before leaving
Communicate the required cleaning of shared walking equipment
why: An agreed route supports mobility while limiting avoidable exposure.
Permission for a planned walk does not automatically authorize a different shared group activity.
Contained drainage and hand hygiene reduce environmental contamination during movement.
A shared equipment-cleaning plan prevents transfer to subsequent users.
takeaway: Plan essential activity within the required transmission precautions.
learningObjective: Plan essential activity within the required transmission precautions.

title: Reusable equipment without instructions
stem: A donated reusable device has no available manufacturer processing instructions. What is best before clinical use?
options: Use the strongest disinfectant available
Copy instructions from a similar-looking device
Obtain validated processing and use information or choose an approved alternative
Rely on intact packaging from the donor
why: Stronger chemicals may damage the device without ensuring appropriate processing.
Similar appearance does not establish compatible materials or methods.
Safe reuse requires a validated process for the actual device.
Donor packaging does not establish clinical readiness.
takeaway: Do not improvise reprocessing for an unfamiliar reusable device.
learningObjective: Do not improvise reprocessing for an unfamiliar reusable device.

title: Processing a critical instrument
stem: Reusable forceps will enter normally sterile tissue. A colleague proposes high-level disinfection to shorten turnaround. Which processing level is required for this use?
options: High-level disinfection after thorough cleaning
Extended immersion in an approved disinfectant
A sterile-water rinse after thorough cleaning
Validated sterilization appropriate to the instrument
why: High-level disinfection is not the required standard for a critical instrument entering sterile tissue.
Longer immersion does not by itself establish a validated sterilization process.
A sterile rinse does not sterilize the cleaned instrument.
Entry into normally sterile tissue requires an appropriate validated sterilization process.
takeaway: Critical instruments require appropriate sterilization before use.
learningObjective: Critical instruments require appropriate sterilization before use.

title: Infection-risk discharge equipment
stem: A client leaving with reusable home equipment can read the instructions but cannot demonstrate the cleaning sequence. What should the nurse arrange before independent use?
options: Demonstrate the device process and observe the client's practice
Give the manufacturer handout and ask for verbal agreement
Explain the process to a caregiver by telephone
Provide the supplier's instructional video for home viewing
why: Observed practice verifies that the client can reproduce the device-specific steps and permits correction.
The client already has readable instructions; agreement does not demonstrate the missing skill.
Caregiver teaching may help but does not establish this client's independent performance.
A video can support learning, but home viewing leaves the identified performance gap unverified.
takeaway: Verify the client's ability to perform device-specific home cleaning.
learningObjective: Verify the client's ability to perform device-specific home cleaning.

title: Safety evaluation after equipment change
stem: A new transfer device has been assessed as suitable for a client. Before staff use it routinely, what evidence best establishes their competence with the new model?
options: Attendance at the introductory device in-service
Observed performance of the correct transfer procedure
Signed acknowledgement of reading the instructions
A shorter average time to complete the first transfers
why: Attendance does not show that staff can correctly perform the required steps.
Direct observation verifies practical technique with the new device.
A reading acknowledgement establishes receipt, not demonstrated performance.
Speed does not establish safe technique or correct use.
takeaway: Evaluate competence and client suitability after equipment changes.
learningObjective: Evaluate competence and client suitability after equipment changes.

title: Inadequate sterilization cycle
stem: A reprocessing alert states that a load did not reach the required sterilization cycle parameters. Several unopened packs from that load are on the unit. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Withhold the affected packs from clinical use
Identify and manage affected items through the recall/reprocessing pathway
Use the packs if their external wrapping remains intact
Notify the relevant team and follow the approved corrective process
why: Inadequate processing means sterility cannot be relied upon.
Load tracing permits appropriate containment and reprocessing.
Intact wrapping cannot compensate for a failed sterilization process.
Coordinated correction prevents exposure and addresses the processing failure.
takeaway: Packaging integrity does not compensate for inadequate sterilization.
learningObjective: Packaging integrity does not compensate for inadequate sterilization.
